title: Take Care of the People, the Products, and the Profits, In That Order
coreMove: Trace financial and product weakness back to the people system before treating profit as a separate target.
sourcePressure: The chapter teaches a causal chain: standards, feedback, training, role clarity, and management quality produce product reliability, which makes profit durable.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version is people-first kindness or morale perks instead of accountable management.

exampleSpecs.domain: specialty bakery expanding wholesale pastry production
exampleSpecs.audience: an owner whose croissant returns look like a flour or oven problem
exampleSpecs.stakes: profit on wholesale accounts is disappearing because shift leads use different proofing standards
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner stops blaming the oven, watches two shift leads proof dough differently, and writes one training standard before repricing accounts
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a rack of collapsed croissants beside two conflicting proofing notes

exampleSpecs.domain: marine electronics repair shop with repeat sonar warranty claims
exampleSpecs.audience: a shop manager tempted to pressure technicians for faster throughput
exampleSpecs.stakes: rushing repairs increases warranty loss and damages dealer trust
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager traces three failed units to the same untrained calibration step and pulls the throughput bonus until every tech passes the bench test
exampleSpecs.firstImage: three returned sonar heads lined up next to a calibration gauge

exampleSpecs.domain: veterinary lab processing biopsy samples across two shifts
exampleSpecs.audience: a lab director seeing late reports and blaming software
exampleSpecs.stakes: delayed diagnoses and lost clinic contracts trace to inconsistent handoff standards
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director follows one sample's path, finds the missing handoff rule between shifts, and retrains supervisors before buying new software
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a biopsy cassette sitting beside a timestamped handoff tray

exampleSpecs.domain: custom furniture manufacturer with margin erosion
exampleSpecs.audience: a founder who thinks profits fell because lumber costs rose
exampleSpecs.stakes: untrained project leads are approving change orders inconsistently
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the founder audits five change orders, finds three different approval rules, and pauses new bids until project leads use one margin gate
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a stack of walnut change orders under a calculator tape

exampleSpecs.domain: regional laboratory instrument sales team missing renewal targets
exampleSpecs.audience: a VP considering commission cuts before checking manager coaching
exampleSpecs.stakes: customers leave because reps cannot explain service intervals clearly
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the VP asks two managers to role-play the renewal explanation, hears the gap, and builds manager certification before changing commissions
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a renewal spreadsheet open beside a service-interval card

exampleSpecs.domain: municipal recycling facility with contamination penalties
exampleSpecs.audience: a plant superintendent blaming residents before checking floor training
exampleSpecs.stakes: penalties rise because sort-line leads apply different rejection calls
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the superintendent stands at two sort lines, records conflicting rejection calls, and creates a lead-training checklist before asking the city for new bins
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a rejected bundle of mixed paper tagged with two different reason codes

skillTargets: trace output problems upstream to management systems
identify management debt before product or profit damage
choose training and standards over superficial morale fixes

tryThisNowSpec: Take one recurring product or financial miss and name the manager behavior, training gap, or unclear standard that could be producing it upstream.
sourceAnchorsNote: source contains no named anecdote for this chapter
